description: Somos uma equipe de programadores e desenvolvedores de jogos e aplicações interativas prontos para encarar o NASA Space Apps Challenge! Temos uma base técnica sólida em código, lógica e na criação de experiências digitais envolventes.
summary:
L.O.G. – Legacy of Giants is a cooperative, hybrid game for two players about the objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Alex flies a ship on a computer screen and sees a picture of the target object, but not its name. Neil holds the cards, printed on 3 A4 sheets or opened as a virtual deck, with real mission data but no picture. The two players talk, compare clues and remove cards until one is left. Then Alex types the position from the card, the ship travels there, and the team adds the object to the catalog. The 25 cards go from the Apollo 11 descent stage to the Ingenuity helicopter and Pioneer 10.

Most students have never heard of these objects, but they are part of the history of exploration. L.O.G. turns real mission data into a conversation, so students learn by reasoning together. It needs only a computer and 3 sheets of paper, and every source is listed in the references.
details:
What it does

L.O.G. – Legacy of Giants is a cooperative game for two players about the objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It is a hybrid game: one part is on a screen and one part is on paper. Each player has only half of the information, so neither player can win alone.

How it works

1. Alex flies the ship, which runs in a web browser on a computer. Alex sees a picture of the target object, but not its name.

2. Neil holds the cards: 3 printed A4 sheets, or the virtual deck, which also opens on a phone. Each card shows real mission data: category, place, mission, size, weight, position, launch year, the year the object was lost and its power source. Each card also has a short fact, told by the object itself. The cards have no pictures.

3. Alex can ask the ship's terminal for clues about size, weight, launch year, year lost, power or mission. Each clue costs experience points (XP), so the team tries to use as few clues as possible.

4. The two players talk. Alex describes the picture and reads the clues. Neil removes the cards that do not fit, until one card is left.

5. That card gives the object's position: latitude and longitude on the Moon or on Mars, or a distance in astronomical units (AU) for objects in space. Alex types it into the navigator. The ship travels there, and the team adds the object to the catalog. Three wrong positions end the mission.

The story

The game has five missions. Between missions, the L.O.G. Operations Center sends messages and reports to the players. Little by little, the reports suggest that Alex is not what Alex believes, and the players start to ask who Alex and Neil really are. When the ship has a sync error, Neil finds the password on the protocol card. Each password comes from a real moment in space history, such as the 1202 alarm during the Apollo 11 landing and "SCE to AUX" during the Apollo 12 launch.

The data

The deck has 25 object cards: 10 on the Moon, 10 on Mars and 5 in space. They are in five categories: rovers and vehicles, landers, probes and telescopes, spacecraft parts and debris, and objects. The deck covers every group of equipment listed in the challenge except the Lunar Roving Vehicles: Apollo lunar modules, ALSEP, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and Kepler. It also has smaller objects, such as the Apollo 11 plaque and the Apollo 15 memorial.

The cards use real mission data, with every source listed in the references. Most values come from NASA sources: the NSSDCA catalog, NASA mission pages, press kits and technical reports. We calculated the distances of the objects in space for 14 November 2026 with NASA JPL Horizons. When NASA does not publish a value, we say so: the size of the Apollo 15 memorial comes from a news article (Slate, 2013), the size of the EASEP is our own estimate from its stowed volume (NASA RP-1036), and two weights are marked "N/A". We checked the values against their sources and corrected our first draft, for example InSight's landing longitude, Viking 2's latitude and Sojourner's power source. Every object picture in the game comes from the NASA Image and Video Library: 19 are real photos of the objects, and 6 are NASA illustrations, a NASA painting or a model. The clues in the terminal are calculated from the same data that is printed on the cards.

Why it matters

Most students have never heard of these objects, but they are part of the history of exploration. The challenge itself notes that school-age space fans usually hear only about active missions. L.O.G. gives students a reason to read real mission data: they need it to win. The game is made for students aged 13 and up, in classrooms, science clubs or at home. A pair of players needs one computer with a web browser and 3 printed A4 sheets, or one computer and one phone. Nothing needs to be installed, and the game is free to play online. The game is in English and Portuguese, so it can also reach students who are still learning English.

What is new

L.O.G. splits the information between a screen and paper. One player has the picture and the other has the data, so the students must describe, ask, compare and decide together. They practice a real science skill: comparing what they observe with what is recorded. The game works like a cooperative "Guess Who?", but every clue is a real fact about a real object. The objects also tell their own stories, because the short fact on each card is written in the first person.

How we built it

- The game: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no game engine, published on itch.io. We used Vite as a local development server.

- The cards: vector graphics (SVG) built by Python scripts from the card data, and exported as PNG files and as a print-ready PDF. The printed set has 27 cards on 3 A4 sheets, double-sided: 25 object cards, 1 protocol card and 1 rules card.

- The languages: one switch on the start screen changes the start screen, the ship and the virtual deck between English and Portuguese.

- Testing: an automated browser test (Playwright) played the first mission from start to end in English, and checked 31 screens for leftover Portuguese text.

- The demo video was recorded from the real game. Its voices are AI-generated (ElevenLabs).

Accessibility, cost and energy

- Cost: one printed set is 3 A4 sheets. The online game is free.

- Devices: the ship needs a computer; on a phone it shows "Not available on phones". The virtual deck works on phones, and the printed cards need no device at all.

- Energy: with printed cards, a pair of players needs only one screen.

- Reuse: one printed set can be shared and used again by many classes.

- Language: English and Portuguese.

What we want to achieve next

- Test L.O.G. with students in schools in Uberlândia and measure what they remember after playing.

- Give missions 2 to 5 their own fixed sets of objects. Today, these missions draw their objects at random from the deck.

- Add the Lunar Roving Vehicles and more objects from NASA's catalogs.

- Publish a short guide for teachers together with the print-and-play cards.

Use of AI

We used AI tools to speed up the work. The voices in the demo video were generated with AI (ElevenLabs). An AI assistant (Claude) helped us write, review and translate texts and parts of the code. Early design drafts of the card frame and of the card back were made with an AI image generator. The final cards do not use those images: the frame was redrawn as vector graphics by code, and the card back uses a real NASA photo (AS12-47-6918). The idea, the game rules and the story are our own. No AI-generated content uses or changes NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
